title: TA9-21296
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the claimant) is a citizen of Albania. He claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The details of the claimant's allegations are documented in his Personal Information Form (PIF)1 narrative and testimony: The claimant started a relationship with a girl, XXXXXX XXXX, in 2009. Her family disapproved of this relationship and approached him on XXXXX, 2009. On that occasion, they beat the claimant and told him to stay away from XXXXXX. The claimant was hospitalised for 26 days because of the beating. After his discharge from hospital, the claimant went into hiding at his grandmother's house. On XXXXXX, 2009, he snuck into the luggage compartment of a bus going to Greece. When it arrived in Greece and the bus driver opened the luggage compartment, he escaped. He found a man who provided him with a fraudulent Latvian passport. The claimant used this passport to travel to Italy and Switzerland before coming to Canada on XXXXXX, 2009. He did not seek protection in Greece, Italy or Switzerland. Rather, he made a claim in Canada. The Hearing

When the panel was questioning the claimant, counsel interjected, asking the claimant whether there was a problem with the interpretation, to which he replied, "Not so far." Counsel alleged that there was a problem in the interpretation with respect to where his grandmother lived, alleging that the interpreter was having a conversation with the claimant which was not being interpreted. As noted by the panel, the interpreter appeared to have been interpreting as required to do, and no such conversation appeared to have been taking place. When the panel asked counsel whether she speaks Albanian, she replied in the negative. Therefore, the panel cannot help but question the basis of counsel's interjection. When the panel asked counsel whether she had any concerns about the interpretation, she replied, "Not so far." The hearing continued without any other concern raised by counsel or the claimant concerning the interpretation.
The determinative issue in regard to this claim is credibility.

The panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee, as he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground in Albania. The panel also finds that the claimant is not a person in need of protection in that his removal to Albania would not subject him personally to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, and in that there are no substantial grounds to believe that his removal to Albania will subject him personally to a danger of torture. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimant established his personal identity and his identity as a national of Albania through his testimony and the document he presented.2 Credibility
On the basis of the cumulative credibility concerns noted below, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not being pursued by the XXXX family as he alleges.

The claimant says that he fears his former girlfriend's brothers because they beat him on XXXXXX, 2009. This incident, therefore, is a material part of the claimant's refugee claim. The panel notes significant inconsistencies and omissions in the claimant's evidence with respect to this incident, as noted below. How was the claimant beaten?

The claimant testified that he was beaten by her two brothers on XXXXXX, 2009. When asked if the brothers used anything to beat him, the claimant stated wooden sticks. Yet, as noted by the panel, the claimant stated in his PIF narrative that her brothers beat him on this occasion with steal bats. The claimant was given the opportunity to explain his inconsistent evidence. He stated that he remembered saying when filling in his PIF narrative that her brothers used wooden sticks, and he does not know why this is not stated in his PIF narrative. The panel does not accept the claimant's explanation. The claimant declared in writing and at the start of the hearing that the content of his PIF was complete, true and correct. In addition, the claimant testified that he understands and reads English to some extent. For instance, he is able to read and understand a newspaper article written in English, though not 100 percent. Significant amendments were made to his PIF narrative, which did not include this discrepancy. As already noted, this incident is material to his refugee claim because it is due to this beating that the claimant fears his former girlfriend's (XXXXXX) brothers. It is reasonable, therefore, to expect his evidence in this regard to be more consistent. Moreover, once there was this inconsistency, it is reasonable for him to not only be aware of it, but amend it accordingly, as he amended other parts of his narrative. His inconsistent evidence in this regard, without reasonable explanation, detracts from his credibility. The claimant suffers a broken arm

It was only in the hearing that the claimant informed the panel, for the first time, that he suffered a broken arm as a result of this beating on XXXXXX, 2009. In support of his refugee claim, the claimant disclosed a medical document3 concerning his injuries. This document provides that the claimant was hospitalised for contusions, lacerations, hematomas and ekinoza. It makes no mention of any broken bones. When the claimant was asked about this, he had no explanation. Given that the medical report refers to the claimant's other injuries, it is reasonable to expect it to have referred to the claimant's broken arm, which it does not. The claimant's inconsistent evidence in this regard detracts from his credibility. How many medical documents did the claimant obtain?

The panel asked the claimant whether he had any document concerning his injuries as a result of the beating. He replied that he submitted it. The claimant disclosed one medical document4. The panel asked the claimant how many medical documents or letters he received, to which he replied, "One" and confirmed that that is the document he disclosed to the Board. He testified that he obtained this document when he was discharged from the hospital on XXXXXX, 2009. He further testified that he did not ask for this document, but it was given to him as a matter of hospital practice in case the patient needs to see another doctor. The claimant's oral evidence in this regard is inconsistent with the information contained in this letter.

The claimant testified that he received this medical document on XXXXXX, 2009; yet, the letter is XXXXXX, 2010, about one year after the claimant says he obtained it. In response, the claimant stated that the document he disclosed to the Board is another document. However, as noted by the panel, the claimant had stated that he only obtained one medical document, which he disclosed to this Board. In response, the claimant stated that he obtained a second document after arriving in Canada. The panel does not accept the claimant's explanation. It was only subsequent to the panel noting the inconsistency between his oral evidence and his written evidence did the claimant's initial oral evidence change. His explanation that he had received a second letter is a further inconsistency because he had initially testified that he only received "one". The claimant's inconsistent and evolving testimony in this regard undermines his credibility. Why was the medical document issued?

Despite having initially stated that he did not request the medical document that he disclosed to the Board, and it was given to him by the hospital as a matter of general practice, after noting the above inconsistency in his evidence, the claimant's testimony then shifted to provide that he requested this letter in 2009 and it was given to his sister. When this was noted by the panel, he stated that he had requested this letter. The panel does not accept the claimant's explanation. It was only subsequent to the panel noting the inconsistency in his evidence did he alter his oral evidence to reflect what is stated in this document. The claimant's evidence, as noted, detracts from his credibility.

When the panel asked the claimant when the letter was given to his sister, counsel immediately interjected telling the claimant that he should say he does not know, if he does not know the answer to a question. The claimant then replied that he did not know. As noted by the panel, there was no reasonable explanation for counsel's interjection at that point in the hearing. Counsel stated that the claimant has a right to be advised that he should say he does not know the answer to a question if this is the case. The panel is cognizant of this and that is why the panel advised the claimant, about 40 minutes earlier at the start of the hearing, that this is what he should do. It is not for the panel to remind the claimant of this throughout the hearing. Moreover, the claimant was assisted by counsel, so it is reasonable to expect that he would have been informed of the hearing process.

This medical document is the central corroborative document the claimant disclosed in his refugee claim. There are several significant concerns with this medical document, as noted. Counsel stated that the panel can enquire with the hospital itself as to its authenticity. It is the claimant's responsibility to present his claim. In light of the credibility concerns noted with respect to this medical document, the panel gives it no weight in terms of establishing the claimant's allegations. XXXXXX family comes to know of the relationship

The claimant testified that XXXXXX never spoke to him about her family's opinion of their relationship. Yet, in his PIF narrative, the claimant stated that when her brothers came to know of their relationship, they were very angry. The panel asked the claimant how he knows this if XXXXXX never told him. He stated that he came to the conclusion that they were angry about the relationship when they beat him in XXXXX 2009. Therefore, not only did the claimant provide a date, but a context. Yet, as noted by the panel, the claimant stated in his PIF narrative that her brothers came to know of their relationship, and were angry about it, in XXXX 2009. The claimant stated that he was not 100 percent sure that they found out in July when he wrote this in his PIF narrative, adding that it was his assumption. When the panel asked him why he wrote this in his narrative but then proceeded to declare its content to be complete, true and correct, he stated that what happened to him was complete and correct. The panel does not accept the claimant's explanation. It is not for the panel to sift through the claimant's evidence, wondering what it based on his speculation and what is not. It was only subsequent to the panel noting this discrepancy did the claimant inform the panel that what he stated in his narrative in this regard is based on his speculation. The claimant's evidence in this regard detracts from his credibility. Contacts while he was in hiding

The claimant testified that, while he was in hiding, he only had contact with one friend, XXXX. He confirmed that he did not have contact with anyone else during this time. Yet, as noted by the panel, the claimant stated in his PIF narrative that, while he was in hiding, he kept "in contact with some of my friends in XXXXXX by phone. My friends told me to stay with my grandmother...because my girlfriend's brothers were still looking for me." (own emphasis added) When this was noted to the claimant, he stated that he had contact with two other friends, but "mostly with XXXX". The panel does not accept the claimant's explanation for his inconsistent evidence. The claimant says in his PIF narrative that he came to know XXXXXX brothers were still looking for him through his friends. It was only after the panel noted this discrepancy did the claimant's oral evidence shift. It is not for the panel to remind the claimant of his written evidence. The core of the claimant's refugee claim is his fear of XXXXXX family. It is reasonable to expect his evidence with respect to the person(s) he was in contact with during his time in hiding and how he came to know they were still looking for him to be more consistent. The claimant's inconsistent and shifting evidence in this regard detracts from his credibility. Failure to Seek Protection Elsewhere

After his departure from Albania, the claimant traveled illegally to Greece, where he stayed for about 15 days, Italy and Switzerland before his arrival in Canada. He did not seek protection in any of these countries because, firstly, Greece is too close to Albania, and, secondly, he was in transit in Italy and Switzerland. The claimant traveled through these countries illegally. He was in these countries that he could be deported from at any time. His failure to seek protection, at his earliest opportunity, is inconsistent with his fear. Significant Amendments

The claimant submitted his PIF on November 26, 2009. He signed and dated his PIF on November 25, 2009, declaring that the contents were complete, true and correct. He was assisted by counsel at the time he completed his PIF. On April 29, 2011, XX months later, the claimant submitted several significant amendments to his PIF narrative concerning days, months and years of when events in his PIF narrative took place as well as where he was living during his time in Albania. The amendments are significant and cannot be overlooked. The panel asked the claimant why he made these amendments, XX months later, after having signed his PIF as noted. He stated that he first gave the information contained in his PIF narrative as he thought it at the time, though it was not correct, adding that he was stressed at the time. The claimant was assisted by counsel and also given the significance of these amendments, it is reasonable that the information contained int he narrative would not have had to have been amended to this extent. The fact that it was, and XX months later, is not reasonable.

Even without disbelieving every part of a claimant's testimony, a panel may find the claimant so lacking in credibility that it concludes there is no credible evidence relevant to his claim.5 A claimant's contradictory testimony can cast doubt upon the totality of his oral evidence.6 This claimant had difficulties in the key areas of his evidence as noted. The panel finds that the claimant is lacking in credibility generally and that this lack of credibility extends to all of the claimant's relevant testimony.

The panel has considered all three protection grounds under s. 96 and ss. 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and, on the basis of the totality of all the evidence made available to the panel, finds that there is not a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted in Albania, nor that he would be subjected personally to a risk to his life, cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture.

For these reasons, the claim is rejected. (signed) "C. Buttigieg" C.
